  <header class="story-heading">
    <p class="story-kicker">COUNTRY COMPARISON · 2021</p>
    <h1>Why Is the Cardiovascular Disease Burden So Different?</h1>
    <p>
      Russia and the United States have dramatically different cardiovascular mortality rates. In 2021, Russia recorded approximately 622.5 cardiovascular deaths per 100,000 people, compared with 273.3 per 100,000 in the United States. This difference raises an important question: what factors might help explain why cardiovascular disease affects populations at such different rates? By comparing behavioral and health-related predictors such as tobacco use, alcohol consumption, physical inactivity, and hypertension, we can investigate whether these factors are associated with differences in cardiovascular mortality around the world.
    </p>
  </header>

  <section class="story-section" aria-labelledby="predictors-heading">
    <div class="story-section-heading">

        <p class="story-kicker">POTENTIAL PREDICTORS</p>
        <h2 id="predictors-heading">What might be associated with the gap?</h2>
      </div>
    </div>
    <p class="story-copy">These figures offer hypotheses to investigate, not a complete explanation. The estimates refer to different years and populations, and comparable U.S. values are not included in the information available here.</p>

    <div class="predictor-grid">
      <article class="predictor-card">
        <p class="predictor-value">44.3%</p>
        <h3>Hypertension</h3>
        <p>Estimated among Russian adults aged 30–79 in 2019. High blood pressure is a major CVD risk factor.</p>
      </article>
      <article class="predictor-card">
        <p class="predictor-value">55%</p>
        <h3>High systolic blood pressure</h3>
        <p>Estimated share of Russia's CVD deaths attributable to high systolic blood pressure in the 2019 profile.</p>
      </article>
      <article class="predictor-card">
        <p class="predictor-value">27.8%</p>
        <h3>Tobacco use</h3>
        <p>Estimated among people aged 15 and older in Russia in 2022.</p>
      </article>
      <article class="predictor-card">
        <p class="predictor-value">~10 g/day</p>
        <h3>Salt intake</h3>
        <p>Estimated average adult intake in Russia in 2019, versus the WHO recommended maximum of 5 g/day.</p>
      </article>
    </div>

    <div class="candidate-factors">
      <h3>Other factors to test</h3>
      <ul>
        <li>Alcohol consumption and harmful use</li>
        <li>Physical inactivity</li>
        <li>Obesity and diet</li>
        <li>Healthcare access and socioeconomic conditions</li>
      </ul>
      <p>These are recognized behavioral, health, or social factors, but this comparison does not show that any one factor caused the Russia–U.S. difference.</p>
    </div>
  </section>

    <p class="chart-caveat">Sources and years differ by measure. “Not provided” means a comparable estimate was not included here; it does not mean the value is zero.</p>

  <aside class="story-caution">
    <h2>Association is not a single-cause explanation</h2>
    <p>Alcohol, tobacco, inactivity, hypertension, diet, obesity, healthcare access, and socioeconomic conditions can overlap and interact. Country-level comparisons cannot establish that one factor explains the entire mortality gap, and they should not be used to infer an individual's risk.</p>
  </aside>
